newsitem.title: USA: Fla. Joint Underwriters plan $300 mln note sale.
newsitem.headline: Fla. Joint Underwriters plan $300 mln note sale.

text.p: Florida's Joint Underwriting Association will make its first entry into the debt market with a $300 million tax-exempt note sale on May 8 via J.P. Morgan Securities, an association spokesman said Monday.
"The JUA goal was to put this in place prior to the start of the 1997 hurricane season on June 1," said associaton spokesman Ron Bartlett.
JUA was created by the Legislature in 1992 to provide windstorm insurance for property owners unable to obtain it from private companies in the aftermath of Hurricane Andrew.

"After Hurricane Andrew you had a situation where 11 property insurance companies went insolvent and there were indications from a number of major insurers that they intended to cancel or non-renew more than 800,000 policies," said JUA spokesamn Ron Bartlett.
"The market continues to be disrupted today in some parts of the state," he said.

The association is run by 13-member board of governors. It is funded via regular assessments paid by insurers who write policies in Floria. If there was ever a deficit, the association could impose an emergency assessment, pro-rated according to each company's market share. That has never been necessary, Bartlett said.
Up to now, the association has relied on a $1.5 billion line of credit from a group of banks led by J.P. Morgan, which expires at the end of 1997.

JUA's board of governors recently acknowledged that "would not be enough to deal with a major hurricane" and is working out a plan to boost its claims paying capabilities to $2.8 billion, Bartlett said.
That includes $300 million from the regular assessments, plus $700 million the JUA would receive from the state's hurricane catastrophe fund if there was a major storm.

JUA is renegotiating a new $1.5 billion line of credit, which will be available for two years and has some limited renewal options. The $300 million issue of "pre-event notes" completes the package, with proceeds to be placed in a trust fund until needed.
"This gives us the ability to have liquidity. At the time a storm hits, the money would be instantly available," Bartlett said.
"If the storm is sufficiently large and the JUA had to go to market for additional borrowing, this has made JUA a known quantity on the world financial markets," he said.

Debt service will be paid from the regular JUA assessments. If the line of credit is tapped, the regular assessments, emergency assessments and catastrophe fund share would all be pledged to pay it off.
Moody's Investors Service Inc has rated the notes A3. A rating from Standard & Poor's Corp is pending.
